name: Karl Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I translate German into English for small firms around here that sell abroad: a brewery, a furniture maker, a company that makes parts for lathes. It's price lists, contracts, the odd website. On Saturdays and Sundays I do phone interpreting shifts for a service that hospitals and police stations call when someone only speaks German. I work at a desk in the corner of the living room while my partner Anja is at the garden centre.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does the money work out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's uneven. One month the brewery wants its whole catalogue done, the next month nothing. The weekend shifts are the steady bit. We'd like to buy a flat one day, but the car needed a new clutch in September and that took everything we'd saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected. The tools help with the boring stuff and that's it. At the brewery I'd be blunt with Mr Weber, the owner. A bad contract costs more than a translator, so the brewery still needs me for the contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but it doesn't change much. The small firms already put their emails through a free tool, so I lose a bit of that work either way. My problem is that the income is lumpy and we've got nothing saved since the clutch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and try to get the brewery onto a monthly retainer, so I've got a fixed amount coming in. I'd use the AI tools a bit more for first drafts of price lists, since other translators say it saves an hour a day. And I'd try to rebuild a small cushion, maybe a hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit restless about money, but that's normal for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a retainer from the brewery look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something like four hundred a month for a set number of pages, and extra beyond that. Mr Weber likes knowing his costs, so he might go for it. It'd mean I could plan for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Anja is at the garden centre. How secure is her job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's seasonal, really. Busy in spring, quiet in winter, and they cut hours in January. So between us we've got two lumpy incomes, which is why I want the retainer.

Rebuild a cushion of **a hundred a month**.
feel: **Fine**, mostly, with normal restlessness about money.

steps.text: Ask Mr Weber for a four-hundred-a-month brewery retainer

Put a hundred a month aside to rebuild the cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and we all have to adjust. I'm not going to cry about it; translators have been worried about computers for thirty years. At the weekend service I'd say to colleagues that phone interpreting will hold up longer than documents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the small firms will do their own price lists and websites with AI. I think I'd lose most of my document work within two years. The weekend shifts might last, but they're not enough to live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to the lathe parts company about a job as an export coordinator, because I already know their customers and products. I'd take a short course in export paperwork and customs. And I'd do more weekend shifts while they're there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not falling apart. I've seen people adjust before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't export coordination also the kind of thinking work AI takes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly, yes. But export coordination is also phoning a lorry driver stuck at a border and sorting it out. That's messier than translation. I'd guess it lasts a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Anja think about you taking an office job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be pleased, honestly. Anja has wanted us both on a regular wage for years. She'd say it's about time we got paid on the same day every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to move fast, because two years isn't time for anyone to retrain. I'm usually in the middle on most things, but this would need proper support. I'd say it at the pub and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my translating is over by 2028 and the phone shifts too. Export coordination might go as well, since it's mostly emails and forms. The only jobs with a few years left are hands-on ones, because the robots come three years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the brewery about a job in production or the warehouse, where the robots come later. Mr Weber's always short of people at bottling time. I'd keep any translation going until it stops, and we'd cut everything we can, starting with the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaken. Not panicking, but properly shaken. I'd feel like I'd wasted my degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Anja the night it was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Anja we'd be fine for a few months and that I'd find something. Then I'd go for a long walk. I'm not sure I'd believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd cut the car. How would you manage without it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The brewery's on the bus route, and Anja could cycle to the garden centre. It's two hundred a month we'd keep. That's the first thing to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan if people start now. I'd tell younger translators not to wait. I'd keep it practical, not political.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd get three good years of translation and phone work, maybe four. Then I'd need something else. I'd rather pick it now than have it picked for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an evening course in brewing or food production in the first year. Mr Weber might take me on part-time while I learn. I'd keep translating for the firms while it lasts and save whatever I can toward the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but there's a path. I like having a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Brewing sounds like a big switch. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've translated every one of the brewery's recipes and tank manuals. I know the words already; I'd need to learn what to do with my hands. And people will still want beer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The languages, mostly. I'd keep them for fun. I'd probably still translate the brewery's labels for nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of warning, so nobody should be caught out. I'd say it to friends, and maybe to the firms I work for, so they plan too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have six or seven more years of translation, with rates sliding. That's long enough to get somewhere with a brewing qualification. It's also long enough to save for the flat, if I'm disciplined.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the document work and phone shifts. I'd use AI tools more, now proven, to take on more firms. I'd do the brewing course part-time from year two or three, and we'd try to save a hundred and fifty a month toward a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish. I'd still lose the job, but I'd have time to land somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you'd lose the job anyway, why use the AI tools more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they'd let me earn more now, while it lasts. More firms, more pages, more money in the deposit pot. It's not loyalty, it's just sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change your plans with Anja?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe we'd get the flat, if we're careful. My partner Anja wants a garden more than anything. I'd like to give Anja that before everything changes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years, nothing saved and everything I do goes at once. What would help is a quick way into a hands-on job, like a paid brewery apprenticeship, and some help with the rent while I learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the small firms. Small businesses like the brewery will be caught out just like translators. The brewery owner doesn't know any of this is coming.

headlineQuote: Small businesses like the brewery will be caught out just like translators. The brewery owner doesn't know any of this is coming.
portrait: Karl is a **27-year-old** German–English translator for local exporters, with weekend phone interpreting shifts.
He lives with Anja, whose **garden centre** job is seasonal; their savings went on a clutch.
Pragmatic and steady, he uses AI **when colleagues prove** it works.
He keeps choosing work that's **messier or hands-on**: export coordination, then brewing.
With more time he feels **in control**; the fast scenario shakes him badly.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because every income stream would go at once with nothing saved.
